articles.title: Dead versus alive
articles.content: WHEN teaching and learning are reduced to imitation, rote learning, technique, or formula, they go dead. They prevent learning from taking place. Students might be able to reproduce thoughts they’ve learned by heart, but they can’t apply that learning in real life or in places where it is supposed to help. They cannot make learning part of themselves and who they are. This type of ‘dead’ learning is shallow and doesn’t go beyond the surface. Students forget it easily too. In fact, many students say they forget the material right after exams or once the semester ends. Movements around the world argue that schools should teach critical thinking, argumentation, debate, and reflection to support deep learning. These are essential skills and abilities that students need to develop. Curricula are designed to facilitate the development of these abilities, but when evaluations are done, we usually find mixed success. What is going wrong? When curricula are reduced to formula-based methods and techniques because teachers care more about getting through the syllabus than ensuring students engage with the learning process, the benefits become limited. Movements around the world even argue for introducing philosophy in schools. As a subject, philosophy is generally regarded as more appropriate for older children. For the most part, it has been taught in the final years of high school or at the university level. But the Philosophy for Children (P4C) movement argues that philosophy should be introduced to younger students. There are many books on content and pedagogy in this area, and philosophy is taught in many schools. One argument for introducing philosophy early concerns its content. People have argued that children need to be introduced to ethics and values early. Philosophy is the best way to introduce these issues, discuss them, and help students make more informed decisions. A philosophical discussion on any topic, such as racism, internet access for children, online bullying, tolerance, respect, etc., could encourage students to think about these important topics and make informed choices about who they want to be and why. People have argued that children need to be introduced to ethics and values early. An equally important argument for introducing philosophy in schools concerns pedagogy and what students will learn by engaging with it. Teaching philosophy is directly linked to introducing debate, argumentation, and critical and analytical thinking in classrooms. Students need to acquire and internalise these skills. For those who support this movement, philosophical discussion is an effective way to develop these skills in students. Of course, there can be critical thinking on any theme — it does not require the subject to be from ethics or metaphysics. But since philosophy has a long tradition of debate and critical thinking, and since ethics and values need to be introduced to children, it might be easier to cultivate critical and analytical thinking through philosophy than through mathematics, physics, or languages. But the key issue is how this is to be done. I have fond memories of my high school physics teacher, who could bring his subject to life by motivating students to approach it with curiosity, questions, and debate. He encouraged us to go deeper with each question and answer, was never impatient when we made mistakes, and was also very open to things he did not know himself. He made physics a joy to study. But in many years of schooling, I had only one such teacher in mathematics and physics, and another in language teaching. The rest — and dozens of teachers taught us over 16-odd years of schooling — were mostly trying to finish the course and give us the needed techniques and information. There was not much joy in how they taught and how we learnt. If anecdote could be evidence, the difference with philosophy teachers was stark. When I studied philosophy at the university level, most of my professors were good at encouraging deep, critical and analytical thinking, allowing time for ambiguity and mistakes, deep learning and very deep engagement with questions. It was pure joy to be part of this experience and benefit from it. I wish every child could have access to such teachers and teaching. Does the subject matter then? Maybe it is not the subject itself but how it is taught in our schools that has led to this difference. Most of our teachers teach languages and mathematics, especially the latter, as dead matter—something to be learned by rote, and reproduced. They do not teach it as matter that requires discovery and exploration. In such cases, introducing philosophy might not work, as even philosophy might be limited to what Plato or Kant said rather than engaging with the subjects they discussed and thought about. Islamiat and Pakistan Studies were introduced in schools here during my student days. Both subjects were taught as content that needed only to be learnt and reproduced rather than as content requiring debate, critical analysis, and argumentation. We see the result in an almost complete lack of intellectual interest in these subjects among students. How do we make teaching and learning alive and vibrant? By embracing debate, critical thought, and argumentation; by exposing students to ambiguity, mistakes, and open discussion; by giving them safe spaces to do so. Unfortunately, all our efforts in education — at the school or university level — in Pakistan are about content transfer, control, and reproduction. How can good thinking survive or thrive in these conditions? The writer is a senior research fellow at the Institute of Development and Economic Alternatives and an associate professor of economics at Lums.
articles.author: Faisal Bari

articles.title: A bleak economic future
articles.content: ROBERT Lucas, a towering figure of 20th-century macroeconomics and a Nobel laureate, opined on economic growth and the standard of living that “the consequences for human welfare involved in questions like these are simply staggering: once one starts to think about them, it is hard to think about anything else” (On the Mechanics of Economic Development, 1988). The context of his observation was the significant differences in standards of living across the globe. I contemplated the same — specifically, whether our economic future might offer us some respite from our perennial failures. Sadly, it does not look good. What follows is a brief narration of various considerations that led me to this conclusion. The incentives and structure of the economy resemble anything but a viable plan for sustained improvement in living standards and chances of shared prosperity. Tellingly, Pakistan now has the unique distinction of being the only country in the world where three different arrangements compete for a limited set of resources. The first is the formal sector, which mainly comprises an extremely unproductive and extractive public sector. The second is the ‘deep state’, growing within the bosom of the public sector (formally and informally) and meeting its growing economic interests through forced ingress. The third is the ‘informal’ sector, estimated at about 35 to 40 per cent of the formal economy, that tries its best to stay away from formality. The implications of continuing this arrangement now and in the future are not well understood. There is little, if any, chance, for example, of an entrepreneur arising who could upend traditional industries and usher in economies of scale or creative disruption. It follows, then, that we will remain stuck with low-productivity, rentier industries like sugar that rely on legislative rents (taxpayer-financed subsidies) and tariff protection to shield them from competition. The incentives and structure of the economy resemble anything but a viable plan for sustained improvement in living standards. An even more damning predicament is the continuation of economic management as merely an accounting exercise to balance the books. From having some of the worst development indicators to the absurdity of taking foreign loans for purposes such as pension reforms, the adverse spillovers of this mediocrity are well known. Yet one is astonished to see such pedestrian management celebrated officially. Witness the bewildering displays of vainglorious puffery under the banner of ‘nationalism’. At the same time, trade with three of our neighbours is almost non-existent, a situation akin to a contraction of the available resource envelope and growth possibilities. This attitude helps explain why we, the world’s fifth most populous country, account for less than 1pc of the massive $35 trillion global trade in goods and services. What we have done to our human capital is another indicator of our dim prospects. Since at least the time of Adam Smith’s seminal work (1776), it has been understood that it is the most valuable input in the process of economic growth, something that Paul Romer’s endogenous growth theory (1990) put an authoritative stamp upon. Developing this input has always remained low on our priorities. An even more grievous spectre now haunts our economy: the flight of quality human capital. It is officially celebrated as an achievement in the context of remittances. Still, no policymaker is willing to realise that the full value of quality human capital is captured outside Pakistan. Think of the innumerable examples of people who have made a name for themselves abroad. What if they had remained here and invested their time, resources, and effort to create wealth at home? Or are we just happy to receive a pittance of that effort in the form of remittances that merely sustain consumption? The ‘Lucas critique’ of the 1970s, which transformed macroeconomics, implies that people respond to policy regimes by revising their expectations. The steady flight of skilled people from Pakistan, a trend since the 1970s, has accelerated sharply in recent decades, suggesting that citizens’ expectations of the country’s future have turned deeply pessimistic. This is reflected in what young people think. Having taught at several universities, I can attest that the majority of students view their education as a stepping stone to settling abroad. For those who cannot make it to foreign shores and are active in the workforce, a difficult predicament under a poorly designed incentive structure awaits. Try justifying, logically, how in a country with one of the lowest labour force participation rates, the salaried class gets bilked for more than Rs2tr of its income in the last five years, while record inflation has decimated purchasing power for the majority. The obvious lesson (which then spills over into expectations) is that the main beneficiary of workers’ effort is the government’s coffers rather than the person. Better then to try one’s luck elsewhere. This hollowing out, which will continue, leaves the public sector and its PSDPs as the major avenue of growth. This system spawns corruption, multi-trillion liabilities, and waste (the burden of which ultimately falls upon the taxpayer). Lahore is the most pertinent example among Pakistani cities, with the second-largest economy and one of the highest per capita incomes. Yet it regularlytops the world’s most polluted city rankingsrather than quality-of-life rankings, thanks mainly to brick-and-mortar-based PSDPs. Any material gains are more than offset by deteriorating air quality and rising health costs. I can continue in this manner — for instance, by pointing out that the legislature is held hostage by the same people who have been there for at least three decades, with no meaningful economic reform emerging during their tenure. It is further compromised by their progeny, who inhabit both Houses. But I am sure the reader gets the gist of my argument: the chances that we will witness a significant turnaround in our economic fortunes are remote. We will likely remain saddled with a state whose main aim, as Marx described it, is ‘nothing else’ other than extracting taxes. At least that’s how I see it. Bob Lucas, I posit, would also have nodded in approval. The writer is an economist. His current research focuses on the long-term analysis of various issues plaguing Pakistan’s economy, as well as economic reforms and the history of economic thought.
articles.author: Shahid Mehmood

articles.title: Selfhood in action
articles.content: THE world we inhabit advances through human endeavours. To be human is to act. Idleness is a cardinal sin of humanity that causes pessimism, dehumanisation, and procrastination — postponing today’s work to tomorrow, which never comes. Idleness tends to stagnate, while action moves the world. What causes developments in the world? Bergson believes in elan vital, Schopenhauer in the will to live, Nietzsche in will to power, and Iqbal in selfhood, each of which explains differently how humanity is driven into the future. Iqbal argues that selfhood in action causes changes in the world. Sir Muhammad Iqbal, a philosopher of human development and action, primarily defends self-development as a means of transforming the potential for action into capability, enabling human agency to be rational, creative, productive, and moral. Iqbal’s philosophy of ‘self-development’ is actually ‘human development’, meaning people have a natural potential to develop, think, and act. To develop is to act. Surprisingly, scholars have not explored Iqbal’s philosophical oeuvre, particularly from the perspective of human development, which Pakistan desperately needs. Action breathes life into ideas. Iqbal writes, “The Quran is a book which emphasises ‘deed’ rather than ‘idea’.” Adam, God’s vicegerent on Earth, was bestowed with infinite potential — creativity, morality, thinking, and action — transmitted to his progeny. According to Iqbal, human beings, as vicegerents, are “God’s co-workers” on the planet. A human is not only a thinker but also an actor and a creator. A human is not only a thinker but also an actor and a creator. Iqbal transforms the idea of Homo sapiens (human, the thinker) into Homo faber (human, the creator) and Homo actor (human, the actor). In The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam, Iqbal states, “the world is not something to be merely seen or known through concepts, but something to be made and remade by continuous action.” Making and remaking the world requires human development, a creative mind, and purposive action. In Asrar-i-Khudi and Rumuz-i-Bekhudi, Iqbal posited his philosophy of ‘human development’. Freedom, self-respect, dignity, love, economic security, courage, education as training, and, above all, action develop the selfhood of the individual and the nation. However, unfreedom, humiliation, exploitation, hatred, economic dependency, threat, torture, and ignorance destroy the selfhood of people. Pakistani intellectual Mahbub ul Haq advanced the idea of human development, arguing for a ‘people-first approach’ in public policy to expand people’s sociopolitical and economic choices. Like Iqbal’s, Mahbub ul Haq’s ideas also deserve attention for improving the quality of people’s lives in Pakistan. Education is the first milestone for human development; any disorder in it means intellectual and moral decadence. The educational system in Pakistan needs revolutionary changes by appointing heads of institutions who are capable of being real agents of transformation rather than just performers on social media. Increasing the budget to promote research and incentives for researchers, and ensuring job security to stop brain drain from the profession of education are also needed. Iqbal articulates: “Action makes life a paradise or a hell/ By nature, a human is neither an angel nor a devil.”A paradise-like life on Earth is possible only with the rule of law, justice, equal distribution of resources, and, particularly, education that fosters the freedom to flourish. Poverty, violence, and ecological decay are pressing challenges to Pakistan and the world. Human development and action are essential to eradicating poverty — meaning that people develop enough capabilities to pursue economic activities as entrepreneurs in IT, AI, arts, and crafts. Peace is essential for life. Peace has two forms: negative and positive. ‘Negative peace’ is the absence of violence, mostly by force. Negative peace is short-term. ‘Positive peace’ refers to life-affirming activities through arts, literature, sports, cultural festivals, and a culture of dialogue. Positive peace is long-lasting. A clean environment sustains life. Littering, pollution, and deforestation create health and aesthetic concerns. Reverence for the environment in individual, social, and institutional conduct is required. Iqbal’s philosophy of human development and action can help meet crucial national and global challenges. Positively, action transforms potential into capabilities, plans into outcomes, possibilities into opportunities, pessimism into optimism, and thought into reality. Action is a supreme virtue, while idleness is a fatal vice. Let people develop and act with freedom for a better future for Pakistan. The writer has a PhD degree from the University of Canterbury, New Zealand, and teaches philosophy at the University of the Punjab, Lahore.
articles.author: Dr Saad Malook

articles.title: Rule of the people?
articles.content: THEresounding defeatof the Republican Party in the US midterm election this week has triggered celebratory chatter around the world. Many see it as the beginning of the end for Donald Trump; the vibe was very similar when Trump wasdefeated by Joe Bidenin the 2020 US presidential election. Yet four years later, Trumpism proved to be alive and very well. Trump cannot stand in the 2028 presidential election. For that reason alone, his political career is reaching its end. But that does not mean that Trumpism — both the ideology and the social base to which it speaks — will disappear alongside the man himself. Here I offer some suggestions what this latest election signals about the future of democracy in the US, and, by extension, around the world. The contemporary state is whittling away democratic freedoms. While progressive ideology has gained a foothold in American society, the Trumpist right maintains its powerful, and mobilisedMAGA base, sustained in part by Christian evangelicals. Before his win in 2024, Trump vowed to stop fighting wars abroad, and bring back industrial jobs and prosperity. His base has been antagonised by the disastrous and prolonged war on Iran, and the inflationary spiral it has triggered. Vice-President J.D. Vance has alreadyacknowledged this, and even added that Washington’s ‘special relationship’ with Israel must change. Trumpism will not die out because of a midterm defeat. Long-term economic stagnation will give it social mooring, while its major ideological enemies — immigration, the left, and outsourcing — remain easy sells. A useful analogy is that of Brazil, where Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva recently staved off the most recent articulation of Bolsanarismo — the parallel ideology to Trumpism — to win his fourth term as president. Brazil’s left has far greater social roots than the emergent Democratic left in the US, hence its ability to mobilise the last-minute votes necessary to re-elect Lula. But the far right under the leadership of the Bolsanaro family also has a mobilised social base, which will rebound from the election loss. Lula is 81, and his Workers Party will have to deepen the social struggle to keep Bolsanarismo at bay in the years to come. Zooming out further, the right wing is ascendant across much of the world, while the contemporary state is whittling away democratic freedoms and paving the way for capital to carry on with business as usual. Electoral victories for left-of-centre candidates in the US, Brazil or wherever else they may come to pass will not produce structural change in isolation. Does going to the ballot allow ordinary people an opportunity to exercise political choice? Yes. But this is not the same as working-class majorities being organised for progressive social transformation. The latter is required both to ensure more significant electoral success and then to turn such victories into substantive change. Of course, we in Pakistan do not even get to enjoy the unfettered right to vote. The military-bureaucratic oligarchy that has ruled over us from soon after 1947 did not even allow a general election until 1970, and then chose military action rather than handing over power to the winning party afterwards. More recently, the electoral mandate in the 2024 general election was stolen blatantly, culminating in theimposition of emergency in KP. There is something to be said for at least the temporary waves of hope that are generated by electoral victories, even if one should at the same time be conscious of the highly delimited nature of democracy under the rule of contemporary capital. Progressives in Pakistan have to fight an epic battle against tyranny to even retain the pretence that democracy means rule of the people. And then we have to come up with a shared project for how to run a country ravaged by violence, repression and a deep crisis of identity. The writer teaches at Quaid-i-Azam University, Islamabad.
articles.author: Aasim Sajjad Akhtar

articles.title: Reviewing ties
articles.content: ALTHOUGH US President Donald Trump has two more years in the White House, theresounding Democratic victoryin Tuesday’s midterm elections, handing both Houses of Congress to the latter party, will have a definite impact on how the American leader deals with both internal issues and foreign relations. For one, the Democrats willstep up legislative scrutinyof Mr Trump’s domestic agenda, as well as his dealings with foreign states. It is likely that many countries, including Pakistan, might have to recalibrate their policies accordingly. The Trump administration’s relationship with Pakistan has been quite warm, with the American president frequentlypraisingthis country’s civil and military leadership publicly. Pakistan’s leadership has returned the compliment, heaping praise on the US leader at international fora, evennominating himfor a Nobel Peace Prize. But with the Democrats clawing back power in Congress, changes in America’s approach to global engagement are likely to occur. Traditionally, the relationship between Pakistan and the Democrats has been complicated, and the country has had an easier time working with the Republicans. For example, bilateral ties during Joe Biden’s administration ranged from lukewarm to ambivalent. Matters changed significantly when Mr Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. Washington’s interest in Pakistan’s crypto and minerals sectors is largely seen as a by-product of the American president’s close ties with the country’s rulers. But as the White House’s internal and external dealings come under greater scrutiny when a Democrat-led Congress starts business in January, Pakistan should be prepared for attitudes to change — and not necessarily for the better. America’shesitationto entertain Pakistan’s request for a $10bn Exchange Stabilisation Support Facility could be a telling sign in this regard. However, even with the Democrats controlling Congress, Pakistan-US ties do not have to nosedive. While relations over the decades have been largely transactional — fighting communism, terrorism, etc — Pakistan should focus on building institutional relations with the US that can weather the storms in Washington. It is true that warm personal ties with whoever occupies the White House can improve relations to a considerable extent. But Pakistan should work with all tiers of the US government — an association that should be based on mutual respect and benefit. Above all, Pakistan must keep its own interest paramount. Durable ties with the US are important, but they should not come at the expense of Pakistan’s other vital relationships, in particular with China. In fact, in the long term, it is in America’s own interest to adopt a more balanced approach in South Asia for the sake of regional stability.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Genuine engagement
articles.content: THE PTI-led opposition alliance TTAP appears to have finally brought an initially reluctant Maulana Fazlur Rahman on board. Or perhaps it was the government that drove him there — through its unfulfilled promises, and the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP. Certain unkind remarks by a federal minister against the maulana might also have helped him make up his mind. Whatever the reason, the JUI-F chief once again finds himself at the centre of efforts to build a united opposition front. On Wednesday, Maulana Fazlur Rahman and opposition leaders led by Mahmood Khan Achakzai held a meeting during which they agreed to coordinate in parliament and raise a unified voice there. That is a welcome development. After all, an opposition that argues on the floor of the House and in parliamentary committees is much better for the political system than one that simply protests on the streets. The opposition must now show that it is willing to engage with the government on essential national issues ranging from electoral reforms to economic priorities. Doing so would place it in a better position to hold the rulers to account for governance failures. A dialogue anchored in legislative debate rather than street agitation offers the only viable path towards mutual concessions, institutional stability, and a way out of the current impasse. Politics is, after all, an exercise in give-and-take. That said, the reality is that the government has given the opposition little reason to engage with it. In fact, it has been justifiably criticised for shrinking the political space for its opponents by passing questionable laws, jailing opposition politicians, and intimidating dissenters. The government’s treatment of dissent as a threat to be contained both inside and outside parliament has understandably left the opposition with little faith in any overture. So the first genuinely conciliatory move must come from the government, which must go beyond its usual rhetoric of being open to talks. Easing pressure on opponents will lessen suspicions and help build trust. The opposition has to reconsider its strategy too. Demonstrations have brought only arrests and little else; each street protest has allowed the government to highlight the issue as a law and order challenge. The government must extend the olive branch, and the opposition should be sensible enough to grasp it.
articles.author: Editorial
